candidate_sources.title: Blue Mold of Tobacco | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Blue mold is a downy mildew disease of tobacco caused by the oomycete Peronospora hyoscyami f.sp. tabacina. The pathogen causes localized lesions appearing as yellow spots that coalesce into light-brown necrotic areas, with gray to bluish downy sporulation on the lower leaf surface. Optimal conditions occur at 60-75Â°F with humidity greater than 95%; the disease is considered a more serious problem in Burley than flue-cured production areas. Includes symptoms, disease cycle, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Peronospora hyoscyami f.sp. tabacina (blue mould of tobacco) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet for Peronospora hyoscyami f.sp. tabacina, the oomycete causing blue mould (downy mildew) of tobacco. Blue mould is one of the most important foliar diseases of tobacco, causing significant losses in the Americas, south-eastern Europe and the Middle East. Covers host range, symptoms, biology, distribution, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco blue mould disease caused by Peronospora hyoscyami f. sp. tabacina | Molecular Plant Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed review (Borras-Hidalgo et al., 2010) describing tobacco blue mould caused by Peronospora hyoscyami f.sp. tabacina. The pathogen causes single or grouped yellow spots that coalesce to light-brown necrotic areas, with sporulation on the lower leaf surface; severe cases involve stem and root infection. Discusses systemic acquired resistance as a key tobacco defence response.

candidate_sources.title: Target Spot of Tobacco | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Target spot is caused by a soil-borne fungal pathogen, Rhizoctonia solani (teleomorph: Thanatephorus cucumeris) species-complex, split into anastomosis groups (AG2-2, AG3, AG4). In the greenhouse, R. solani causes 'damping off' or soreshin, inhibiting seed germination or causing seedling collapse; the lower stem has sunken, reddish-brown lesions. AG-3 causes 'sore shin' and 'target spot' in mature plants, with water-soaked lesions on leaves extending up the stem. Includes management with azoxystrobin and mancozeb foliar sprays and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizoctonia solani (Target spot of Tobacco) - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia solani AG-2-2 and AG-3 infect tobacco seedlings causing damping off and stem rot; AG-3 causes 'sore shin' and 'target spot' in mature plants. The pathogen overwinters on plant residue and soil. Small (2-3 mm) white to tan spots develop on lower leaves closest to the soil. Covers symptoms, pathogen biology and management for flue-cured and burley tobacco.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco leaf spot and root rot caused by Rhizoctonia solani KÃ¼hn - PMC
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizoctonia solani causes damping off and stem rot in young transplants, sore shin in older field plants, and a foliar disease named 'target spot'. All cultivars of flue-cured and burley tobacco are susceptible to target spot. Reviews pathogen anastomosis groups, symptoms and management.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) | Burley Tobacco Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Tomato spotted wilt virus symptoms vary with plant age, with plants frequently being stunted and leaves becoming distorted due to uneven growth of foliage. Necrotic (brown) zonate spots and rings may occur on younger leaves, and spots may merge together to form larger necrotic areas. TSWV is a member of the genus Orthotospovirus, a group of plant viruses vectored by thrips. Management approaches are host resistance, vector control or avoidance.

candidate_sources.title: New Factsheet: Managing TSWV and Thrips in Tobacco | NC State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Tobacco thrips are of most significant concern as vectors of Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV). Only larval-stage thrips can acquire the virus when feeding on infected plants. Management includes at-planting neonicotinoid insecticides such as imidacloprid, resistant varieties, and an integrated IPM strategy for thrips and TSWV in tobacco.

candidate_sources.title: Scouting for Tobacco Thrips and Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus | NC State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: TSWV infections cause the most damage to plants when they occur within the first six weeks following transplant, although symptoms may not develop for a few weeks after infection. If infection becomes systemic, the bud may be infected and the plant often exhibits classic bilateral wilting, with small dark-colored ringspots on foliage. Covers scouting for tobacco thrips, the vector of TSWV.
